questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This figure contrasts the lobes of the right and left lungs. Why does the left lung have fewer lobes than the right?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The diaphragm rises higher on the left, compressing a lobe

choices.label: B
choices.text: The left main bronchus fails to branch during development

choices.label: C
choices.text: The left lung is supplied by only one pulmonary artery

choices.label: D
choices.text: The heart occupies space on the left (the cardiac notch)

choices.label: E
choices.text: The left lung lacks a visceral pleura over its middle region

explanation.summary: The right lung has three lobes (superior, middle, inferior) while the left has two (superior, inferior). The heart's leftward position creates the cardiac notch and lingula, leaving space for only two lobes on the left.
explanation.whyCorrect: The right lung has three lobes (superior, middle, inferior) while the left has two (superior, inferior). The heart's leftward position creates the cardiac notch and lingula, leaving space for only two lobes on the left.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This figure highlights the root (hilum) of the lung. What is the functional significance of this region?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the region that produces surfactant to reduce surface tension

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is where the two pleural layers become continuous with the diaphragm

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the site of gas exchange between alveoli and capillaries

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is where the bronchus, pulmonary vessels, and nerves enter and leave the lung

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the point at which the trachea divides into main bronchi

explanation.summary: The hilum (lung root) is the medial gateway where the main bronchus, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, lymphatics, and nerves pass between the mediastinum and the lung.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hilum (lung root) is the medial gateway where the main bronchus, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, lymphatics, and nerves pass between the mediastinum and the lung.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This diagram maps the lymph nodes draining the lungs. Why is knowledge of this drainage pattern clinically important?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It identifies the sites where oxygen enters the bloodstream

choices.label: B
choices.text: It locates the pacemaker cells that set respiratory rhythm

choices.label: C
choices.text: It predicts the pathway by which lung cancer spreads

choices.label: D
choices.text: It marks where the phrenic nerve stimulates the diaphragm

choices.label: E
choices.text: It shows where surfactant is reabsorbed after each breath

explanation.summary: Bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes drain to mediastinal and then supraclavicular nodes. This orderly pattern determines how bronchogenic carcinoma metastasizes and underlies lymph-node staging.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes drain to mediastinal and then supraclavicular nodes. This orderly pattern determines how bronchogenic carcinoma metastasizes and underlies lymph-node staging.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: The magnified inset shows the two pleural layers with a thin gap between them. What is the primary function of this pleural space?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It stores reserve air used during forced expiration

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the main site of oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange

choices.label: C
choices.text: It generates the negative pressure by secreting surfactant

choices.label: D
choices.text: It houses the lymph nodes that drain the lung parenchyma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its thin fluid film couples the lung to the chest wall

explanation.summary: The visceral and parietal pleurae are separated by a thin serous fluid film. Surface tension of this fluid keeps the lung apposed to the chest wall while allowing frictionless sliding; the costodiaphragmatic recess provides expansion room during inspiration.
explanation.whyCorrect: The visceral and parietal pleurae are separated by a thin serous fluid film. Surface tension of this fluid keeps the lung apposed to the chest wall while allowing frictionless sliding; the costodiaphragmatic recess provides expansion room during inspiration.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This resin cast fills the hollow airways down to their finest branches. What anatomical structure is being displayed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pulmonary arterial tree

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pulmonary venous network

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bronchial artery circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The thoracic lymphatic vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: The bronchial tree

explanation.summary: The cast shows the trachea dividing at the carina into main bronchi that branch repeatedly into progressively smaller bronchi and bronchioles, forming the tree-like conducting airways of the lungs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cast shows the trachea dividing at the carina into main bronchi that branch repeatedly into progressively smaller bronchi and bronchioles, forming the tree-like conducting airways of the lungs.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: The trachea divides at the carina into the primary bronchi shown here. Why is an aspirated foreign body more likely to lodge in the right main bronchus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The left bronchus has stronger ciliary clearance

choices.label: B
choices.text: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left

choices.label: C
choices.text: The right bronchus lacks protective cartilage rings

choices.label: D
choices.text: The right bronchus branches before reaching the lung

choices.label: E
choices.text: The left bronchus is guarded by the epiglottis

explanation.summary: Because the right main bronchus descends at a steeper, more vertical angle and has a larger caliber, gravity directs aspirated material into it more often than into the more horizontal left bronchus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the right main bronchus descends at a steeper, more vertical angle and has a larger caliber, gravity directs aspirated material into it more often than into the more horizontal left bronchus.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: Each colored region of these lungs is fed by its own tertiary bronchus and artery. What are these functionally independent units called?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alveolar sacs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bronchopulmonary segments

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pleural recesses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pulmonary lobules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pulmonary acini

explanation.summary: A bronchopulmonary segment is supplied by a single segmental (tertiary) bronchus and segmental artery. Because each is a discrete unit, a diseased segment can be surgically resected without disrupting its neighbors.
explanation.whyCorrect: A bronchopulmonary segment is supplied by a single segmental (tertiary) bronchus and segmental artery. Because each is a discrete unit, a diseased segment can be surgically resected without disrupting its neighbors.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: On this normal PA chest radiograph, why do the lung fields appear dark (radiolucent) compared with the central heart shadow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone in the lung fields scatters the beam away from the detector

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lungs contain dense muscle that blocks the X-ray beam

choices.label: C
choices.text: The heart emits radiation that exposes the surrounding film

choices.label: D
choices.text: The air-filled lungs absorb little radiation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contrast dye has been injected into the pulmonary vessels

explanation.summary: Air is far less radio-dense than soft tissue or bone. X-rays pass easily through the air-filled alveoli and expose (darken) the film, whereas the muscular, blood-filled heart absorbs the beam and appears white.
explanation.whyCorrect: Air is far less radio-dense than soft tissue or bone. X-rays pass easily through the air-filled alveoli and expose (darken) the film, whereas the muscular, blood-filled heart absorbs the beam and appears white.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: The pretreatment chest X-ray (arrow) shows homogeneous white opacity blunting the right costophrenic angle that clears after treatment. What abnormality does this most likely represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lobar pneumonia consolidation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cardiomegaly

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pleural effusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pulmonary fibrosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tension pneumothorax

explanation.summary: Fluid in the pleural space (pleural effusion) is dense and layers dependently, producing a white opacity that blunts the costophrenic angle. Drainage or treatment restores the normal dark, air-filled lung seen post-treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluid in the pleural space (pleural effusion) is dense and layers dependently, producing a white opacity that blunts the costophrenic angle. Drainage or treatment restores the normal dark, air-filled lung seen post-treatment.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: The airways from the trachea through the terminal bronchioles are grouped as the 'conducting zone.' What physiological property defines this zone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the primary site of oxygen–carbon dioxide exchange

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is lined entirely by gas-exchanging alveoli

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is where pulmonary capillaries first contact air

choices.label: D
choices.text: It actively secretes surfactant to reduce surface tension

choices.label: E
choices.text: It carries air but performs no gas exchange

explanation.summary: The conducting zone (trachea to terminal bronchioles) warms, humidifies, and channels air but has no alveoli, so it constitutes anatomic dead space. Gas exchange begins only in the respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and sacs).
explanation.whyCorrect: The conducting zone (trachea to terminal bronchioles) warms, humidifies, and channels air but has no alveoli, so it constitutes anatomic dead space. Gas exchange begins only in the respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and sacs).

questions.imageRef: repic-619_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract_p10_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Lower Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This overview divides the airway into a conducting zone and a respiratory zone. What distinguishes the respiratory zone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It comprises the trachea and main bronchi that transmit air

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the region cleared by the mucociliary escalator alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: It warms, humidifies, and filters incoming air only

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is lined by vocal cords that generate sound

choices.label: E
choices.text: It contains alveoli where gas exchange actually occurs

explanation.summary: The conducting zone (nose through terminal bronchioles) transports, warms, and cleans air but has no alveoli. The respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and sacs, alveoli) is where oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the blood-gas barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: The conducting zone (nose through terminal bronchioles) transports, warms, and cleans air but has no alveoli. The respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and sacs, alveoli) is where oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the blood-gas barrier.
